title: Good Stabilizer Codes from Shallow Clifford Circuits with Random Matchings
authors: Emile Anand, Elia Gorokhovsky, Jennifer Hritz, Jingtong Sun
abstract: Encoding quantum information with low circuit overhead is a fundamental challenge in fault-tolerant quantum computation. Random circuits provide a natural mechanism for rapidly spreading logical information through simple gates applied in parallel. Brown and Fawzi showed that random Clifford circuits on two-qubit Clifford gates provide such encoders that achieve the quantum Gilbert-Varshamov rate-distance tradeoff with depth $O(\log^3 n)$. We show that the same asymptotic tradeoff is attained in optimal $O(\log n)$ depth under a gate distribution with a more restricted support. For every fixed $δ>0$ and sufficiently large $n$, if $\frac kn < 1 - H(\frac{d}{n}) - \frac{d}{n}\log_2 3 - δ$, we can construct random circuits of depth $O(\log n)$ which define, with high probability, an $[n,k]$ stabilizer code of distance at least $d+1$, which matches the $Ω(\log n)$ light-cone lower bound for linear distance encoders. Our ensemble employs a random matching circuit architecture consisting of $T$ independent permutation-invariant layers. In each layer, the qubits are paired up by a uniformly random perfect matching, and a random independent two-qubit Clifford gate is applied to each pair. The gate distribution need not be uniform over, or even have full support on, the two-qubit Clifford group; rather, we allow for very general distributions on Clifford gates satisfying three regularity conditions. In particular, the construction can be implemented using $n/2$ CNOT gates on randomly matched pairs in each layer, with parallel one-qubit Clifford twirls. These regularity conditions allow us to reduce the second-moment dynamics of our random circuits to a reversible Markov chain on binary support strings. We establish logarithmic hitting-time bounds for this Markov chain and comparisons of its stationary distribution to prove the coding properties of the circuits.
summary: This paper develops a method to construct high-performance quantum error-correcting codes using shallow random circuits. By employing a random matching circuit architecture, the authors prove that the optimal rate-distance tradeoff can be achieved with a circuit depth scaling only logarithmically with the number of qubits. This advances the feasibility of fault-tolerant quantum computation.
main_problem: The core challenge is constructing quantum error-correcting codes with minimal circuit depth while achieving the optimal quantum Gilbert-Varshamov rate-distance tradeoff.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that random matching circuits can achieve the optimal rate-distance tradeoff with a depth of only $O(\log n)$, significantly improving upon previous results.
method: The construction uses a random matching circuit architecture over $T$ layers, analyzing the resulting code properties by reducing the dynamics to a reversible Markov chain on binary support strings.
model_or_system: The system involves encoding quantum information on $n$ qubits using random Clifford circuits composed of layers where qubits are paired by a random perfect matching, and a random two-qubit Clifford gate is applied to each pair.
key_observables: Code parameters include the length $n$, dimension $k$, and minimum distance $d$; the depth $T$ is a key observable.
important_parameters: The rate-distance tradeoff parameters ($k/n$ vs $d/n$), the depth $T=O(\log n)$, and the required regularity conditions on the gate distribution $p_2$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the gate distribution satisfies three regularity conditions (bi-invariance, positive entanglement, reversibility) and relies on bounding the hitting time of the associated Markov chain.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem, presents the random matching circuit model, analyzes the coding properties using Markov chain theory (hitting time bounds), and finally proves the rate-distance tradeoff by showing the depth $O(\log n)$ is sufficient.
why_interesting: The focus on shallow circuits and achieving fundamental bounds like the GV tradeoff is central to building fault-tolerant quantum computers, which is a major area of theoretical quantum physics.
